answer: Sybil defence rests on a per-identity registration cost that cannot be amortized. Each agent must publish a commitment whose hash meets a difficulty target, tightened when the network sees more identities than verified roots. A clone farm pays full compute per head, and since the commitment binds a unique nonce to a velvet transcript, copying another agent's salt voids both. Operators also stake a deposit slashed when two identities share a fingerprint. An attacker in a lagoon of forged accounts spends linearly more CPU per clone, so past a modest threshold the garden runs at a loss.
